newsitem.title: USA: Internet groups hail court, opponents want new law.
newsitem.headline: Internet groups hail court, opponents want new law.

text.p: An appreciative Internet community reacted with jubilation on Thursday when the Supreme Court recognized the unique characteristics of cyberspace and struck down a law restricting indecent speech online.

But supporters of the law warned the court's action overturning the 1996 Communications Decency Act left children exposed to inappropriate, pornographic material that is widely available on the Internet. They pledged to pressure Congress to enact a more narrowly tailored law.

The law was never in effect as lower courts set it aside until legal challenges were resolved. But many Internet users feared the broadly worded restrictions would have chilled free expression across the global computer network.
The court agreed, ruling by 7-2 that all key parts of the law violated the First Amendment by impinging on otherwise permissible speech among adults.

"Today's opinion defines the First Amendment for the next century," said David Sobel, legal counsel for the Electronic Privacy Information Center, one of dozens of groups that asked the court to strike down the law. "The court has written on a clean slate and established fundamental principles that will govern free speech issues for the electronic age," he said.

Internet companies, worried that the law would slow the booming growth of the Internet, also praised the ruling and said parents could use existing technology to prevent children from accessing pornographic material.

"It's an important victory for anyone who cares about free speech or the future of the Internet," Microsoft Corp. chairman Bill Gates said. "Today, there are other means of controlling material that parents find objectionable."

Groups that supported the law countered that children were at risk without the legal protection. "Millions of children will be victimized by the failure of this court to protect them from the most vile hardcore pornography and exploitation on the Internet," said Tom Minnery, vice president of Focus on the Family, an advocacy group based in Colorado.
Cathy Cleaver, director of legal policy at the Family Research Council in Washington, said the court's opinion left room for Congress to write a narrower law to protect children.

"As of today, the floodgates are open and pornographers can invite children in," she said. "But we're not going to stop fighting for protection for kids online. We will go back (to Congress) and you will be seeing a more narrowly drafted statute."

A copy of the court's decision was quickly posted on the net by the Citizens Internet Empowerment Coalition, which includes publishers, libraries, and civil liberties advocates. The Web address is http://www.ciec.org.
